'''Raith Rovers Football Club''' is a Scottish professional [[association football|football]] club based in the town of [[Kirkcaldy]], [[Fife]]. The club was founded in 1883 and currently competes in the {{Scottish football updater|RaithRov}} as a member of the [[Scottish Professional Football League]].

The club has won five national trophies: the [[1994 Scottish League Cup final|1994 Scottish League Cup]], and the [[2013–14 Scottish Challenge Cup|2013–14]], [[2019–20 Scottish Challenge Cup|2019–20]], [[2021–22 Scottish Challenge Cup|2021–22]] and [[2025–26 Scottish Challenge Cup|2025–26]] editions of the [[Scottish Challenge Cup]], and were runners-up in the [[1949 Scottish League Cup final (March)|1949 Scottish League Cup]] and [[1913 Scottish Cup final|1913 Scottish Cup]]. They have won the second tier of Scottish football six times, been runners-up four times, and reached its highest ever league finish in [[1921–22 in Scottish football|1922]], third in [[Scottish Football League|Division One]].

As a result of winning the League Cup in 1994, Raith Rovers qualified for European football for the first time, entering the [[UEFA Cup]] the following season. The club managed to reach the [[1995–96 UEFA Cup#Second round|second round]], only to be defeated 4–1 [[Two-legged tie|on aggregate]] by eventual champions [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]].

Raith's home ground is [[Stark's Park]], an {{SPFL-stadiums|raith}} [[all-seater stadium]] in the south of [[Kirkcaldy]].<ref name="capacity">{{cite web |url=https://spfl.co.uk/clubs/raith-rovers/ |title=Raith Rovers Football Club|publisher=Scottish Professional Football League |access-date=11 November 2013}}</ref> The club has been based at the ground since 1891.

==History==

===Beginnings and name===
[[File:Stark's Park - geograph.org.uk - 204446.jpg|thumb|right|Stark's Park, home of Raith Rovers]]
The modern Raith Rovers were founded in 1883 in the Scottish town of Kirkcaldy, playing first at Sands Brae,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Eunson |first1=Eric |title=Old Kirkcaldy: Central, North and West |date=1998 |publisher=Stenlake Publishing |location=Catrine, East Ayrshire |isbn=1-84033-052-X |page=29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kirkcaldyin50objects.com/copy-of-the-sea-wall|title=Raith Rovers|website=50objects}}</ref> now part of the [[Esplanade]], then [[Kirkcaldy#Culture|Robbie's Park]]. Though there were other teams who incorporated the town name, such as Kirkcaldy Wanderers and [[Kirkcaldy United F.C.|Kirkcaldy United]], Raith became the most successful of the local teams, winning five trophies in the 1890s.<ref name="Kirkcaldy Remembered" /> There had been a much earlier (and unrelated) Raith Rovers which merged with what is now [[Cowdenbeath F.C.|Cowdenbeath]] in 1882.

Although it lends its name to many entities in the region, Raith is not itself a settlement. A Raith Rovers victory in the 1960s led to a [[BBC]] [[Colemanballs|commentator's blunder]] that the fans would be "dancing in the streets of Raith tonight". Although commonly attributed to [[David Coleman]], it was actually said by [[Sam Leitch]].<ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration" /> [[Raith, Fife|Raith]] ({{langx|gd|[[Ringfort|rath]]}}, "fort" or "fortified residence") as an area once stretched from south of [[Loch Gelly]] as far as Kirkcaldy<ref>{{cite book|last=Taylor|first=Simon|title=The Place-Names of Fife, Volume One|year=2006|publisher=Shaun Tyas|isbn=1-900289-77-6|pages=496|author2=Gilbert Markus }}</ref> and the [[Battle of Raith]] was once theorised to have been fought here in 596 AD.<ref name="Kirkcaldy Remembered">{{cite book
 | author = Kirkcaldy Civic Society
 | title  = Kirkcaldy Remembered, 2nd edition
 | year   = 2007
 | isbn   = 978-1-84588-386-7}}</ref>
Raith House and Raith Tower sit on Cormie Hill to the west of Kirkcaldy and several parts of the town are built on land formerly of the Raith Estate,<ref>{{cite book|title=Kirkcaldy's Famous Folk, Volume 3|year=2000|publisher=Kirkcaldy Civic Society|pages=13}}</ref> although the modern housing estate bearing the Raith name dates from long after the origins of the team.

A mixture of local success and ambition took the club into the senior leagues where they established themselves and thereby became the pre-eminent team in the town. The club became a senior team in 1889 around the same time they were forced to leave Robbie's Park which was incorporated into a new public park called the [[Beveridge Park]], named after Provost Michael Beveridge.<ref name="Kirkcaldy Remembered" /><ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration" />
The team subsequently moved to their current home of [[Stark's Park]] named after and run by councillor Robert Stark in 1891.<ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration">{{cite book
 | author = Kirkcaldy Civic Society
  | title = Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration
  | publisher = The Francis Firth Collection
  | year = 2005
  | isbn = 1-84567-749-8}}</ref>
The club turned professional by 1892 and were the first football team in Fife to be elected to the [[Scottish Football League|Scottish League]] in season 1902–03.<ref name="Kirkcaldy Remembered" /><ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration" />
The club were incorporated into a limited company: the Raith Rovers Football and Athletic Company, Ltd in 1907. After two consecutive successful seasons in [[Scottish Football League Second Division|2nd Division]], the club elected to join the [[Scottish Football League First Division|1st Division]] in 1909–10. Three years later, the club made their first (and only) appearance in the [[Scottish Cup]] Final, losing 2–0 to [[Falkirk F.C.|Falkirk]].

===Setting records===
In 1921 an innovation in training, previously unknown to the Scottish game, was introduced by directors following a visit to England: the use of a ball in training. As noted in the [[Fife Free Press]], "Hitherto, ball practice has been an absentee from the training curriculum on the grounds that being away from the ball for a week imparted eagerness on the Saturday." This heralded an era of success.<ref name=Stramash>{{cite book|last=Gray|first=Daniel|title=Stramash|year=2010|publisher=Luath Press|location=Edinburgh|isbn=978-1-906817-66-4|pages=109–110}}</ref>

The club had its highest ever league finish in the Scottish top division, when they came third to the Old Firm in [[1921–22 Scottish Division One|1921–22]] under manager [[James Logan (forward, born 1885)|James Logan]]<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3FBuAwAAQBAJ&q=james+logan+raith+rovers&pg=PA229|title=Gaffers| page=229|author=David Ross |isbn=9780743429917 |publisher=[[Lulu.com]] |year=2013|access-date=12 November 2018}}</ref>{{self-published inline|date=February 2020}} (a former Raith player who had fought in [[World War I]] having enlisted in [[McCrae's Battalion]], along with several teammates who died in the conflict).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fifetoday.co.uk/news/raith-ww1-strip-ensures-kirkcaldy-never-forgets-1-3389954|title=Raith WW1 strip ensures 'Kirkcaldy never forgets'|work=Fife Today|date=26 April 2014|access-date=12 November 2018|archive-date=12 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181112181809/https://www.fifetoday.co.uk/news/raith-ww1-strip-ensures-kirkcaldy-never-forgets-1-3389954|url-status=dead}}</ref> This was followed by the unusual incident where the players were shipwrecked in 1923.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b09dhfnb|title=Raith Rovers Shipwreck and the Scottish Inquisition, Series 2, Time Travels - BBC Radio Scotland|website=BBC}}</ref> Along with a cargo of chilled meat bound for [[Buenos Aires]], the team had been en route to play friendly matches on the [[Canary Islands]] when the SS ''Highland Loch'' ran aground off the coast of [[Galicia (Spain)|Galicia]], near [[Vilagarcía]]. The players were able to safely disembark, being rescued by local fishermen.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.raithrovers.net/62760/raith-rovers-shipwrecked.htm|title=Raith Rovers – The Team That Was Shipwrecked | Raith Rovers FC|website=Raithrovers.net}}</ref> They continued on their way a few days later,<ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration"/> winning all four of their games on the islands, including one against [[Third Lanark]], returning from a tour of South America.<ref name=autogenerated1 /> In July 2023, the club marked the 100th anniversary of the shipwreck with its new away strip in the yellow and blue colours of [[UD Las Palmas]], a team based in Gran Canaria, and including a map of the archipelago and the date of the shipwreck.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Williams |first1=Craig |title=Shipwrecked Scots football club gains new followers in Spain |work=The Herald |date=27 July 2023 |location=Glasgow |page=3}}</ref>

The team battled on during tough times between the 1920s and 1930s but things improved by the season of 1937–38, which saw Raith setting a British League Record with 142 goals in just 34 league matches while winning the 2nd Division championship.<ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration" /> The record still stands today. The forward line of Glen (5 goals), Gilmour (35), [[Norrie Haywood]] (47), Whitelaw (26) and Joyner (21) scored 134 of the record 142 goals.

Around this time, a then record crowd of 25,500 filled Stark's Park on a Wednesday afternoon for a Scottish Cup quarter-final replay against East Fife (The first game had attracted 19,000 to the old Bayview ground). East Fife won 3–2 and went on to become the only 2nd Division club to win the Scottish Cup until Hibs matched the feat in 2016.

Record appearance holder [[Willie McNaught]] first appeared for Raith during the war before signing on a contract basis when normal football resumed after the end of global hostilities. McNaught went on to make 657 senior football appearances (many as captain) for Rovers. Raith reached the League Cup final for the first time in 1948–49 but lost 2–0 to [[Glasgow Rangers FC|Rangers]]. In an echo of what would happen four decades later, the club also went on to win the 2nd Division title. In the period of the club's greatest high level consistency, Rovers stayed in the top division until the season after McNaught's 1962 departure. In 1951, Raith had their largest ever gate for a Scottish Cup semi-final at [[Hampden Park]] watched by a crowd of 84,640. Raith lost 3–2 to [[Glasgow Celtic FC|Celtic]].

===Promotions, relegations and ''Footballer of the Year''===
A disastrous season came in 1962–63, when the club finished bottom of the First Division conceding 118 goals in 34 games.<ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration" />
After leaving [[Queen of the South F.C.|Queen of the South]], [[George Farm]] became Raith manager in 1964.<ref name=autogeneratedqos>{{Cite web|url=http://www.qosfc.com/new_legendsview.aspx?playerid=1051|title=QosFC: Legends - George Farm|access-date=8 June 2013|archive-date=3 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130603150440/http://www.qosfc.com/new_legendsview.aspx?playerid=1051|url-status=dead}}</ref> Farm took Raith to promotion in 1966–67 before leaving for Fife rivals [[Dunfermline Athletic F.C.|Dunfermline Athletic]] and was never able to repeat the formula when he returned in the season of 1971–72.<ref name="Rovers Recalled">{{cite book | last = Litster | first = John | title = Rovers Recalled: Raith Rovers in pictures through the years, Volume 1 | year = 2002 | publisher = John Litster | isbn = 0-9534682-1-6}}</ref>
Raith managed to avoid relegation in 1967–68, thanks to [[Striker (association football)|striker]] [[Gordon Wallace (Scottish footballer)|Gordon Wallace]], who became the first player outwith the Old Firm to be voted [[SFWA Footballer of the Year]]. He scored 27 goals in 34 matches.<ref name="Rovers Recalled" /> However the club did find themselves being relegated again at the end of the 1969–70 season.<ref name="Rovers Recalled" /> Nonetheless, the Rovers during this time managed to get through to the quarter-finals of the Scottish cup for the second year running between 1970–71 and 1971–72 – although the latter saw them beaten 3–1 by [[Kilmarnock F.C.|Kilmarnock]] with a crowd of 10,815.<ref name="Rovers Recalled" />

In 1975–76, the league set-up changed from Divisions 1 & 2 to a 3 tier system (Premier Division, Division 1 & Division 2). In the inaugural year of this system, Raith were promoted to the 1st Division, but were promptly relegated the next season, before bouncing back up the season after. Raith then performed reasonably well in the 1st Division, hovering around the top four until the early 1980s.

A new manager, [[Frank Connor]] took charge in early 1986, bringing many new faces onto the team which resulted in promotion on goal difference after a 4–1 win against Stranraer (while [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]] lost to [[Stirling Albion F.C.|Stirling Albion]]) on the last day of the season.<ref name="Rovers Recalled" />

===The League Cup winning era===
Raith reverted to being a full-time side again for the season of 1991–92 which was soon followed by winning the First Division title in the season of 1992–93.<ref name="Rovers Recalled" /> This was to start the most successful period in the club's history – which saw the team's first foray into the [[Scottish Premier Division]] (now the Premiership).<ref name="RRFC 1991-92-1995–96">{{cite book
  | last = Fimister
  | first = Tony
  | title = Raith Rovers Football Club 1991–92 – 1995–96
  | publisher = Tempus Publishing Ltd
  | year = 2002
  | isbn = 0-7524-2425-4}}</ref>

On 27 November 1994, Raith, managed by Jimmy Nicholl, surprisingly beat Celtic 6–5 on penalties to win the [[1994 Scottish League Cup final|Coca-Cola Cup]], after a 2–2 draw.<ref name="Kirkcaldy Remembered"/><ref name="Kirkcaldy: A History and Celebration" /> Future Raith manager, [[Gordon Dalziel]], scored the equalising goal for Raith in the dying minutes of regulation time. The same season, Raith were again promoted to the Premier Division after winning the First Division title.

As a result of the Cup win, Raith qualified for Europe ([[UEFA Cup]]) for the first time in their history. After eliminating both the [[Faroes]]e and Icelandic champions ([[Gøtu Ítróttarfelag]] and [[Íþróttabandalag Akraness]] respectively) in the first two rounds, the club finally succumbed to eventual UEFA Cup winners [[Bayern Munich]]. They were beaten 2–0 by the [[Football in Germany|German]] side in the 1st leg, which was not played at their home ground but at [[Easter Road]], home of [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]]. In the 2nd leg, at the [[Olympic Stadium (Munich)|Olympiastadion]] they led 1–0 at half time against all odds, eventually losing 2–1.<ref name="Rovers Recalled" /><ref name="FCBscot25">{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/feb/12/bayern-munich-celtic-champions-league-play-offs|title=Bayern’s Scottish adventures: from wrath against Raith to a shock at Aberdeen|work=The Guardian|author=Ewan Murray |date=12 February 2025 |access-date=12 February 2025}}</ref> This was the first time a Scottish team had qualified for a major European competition while playing outside the top league. The same season, Raith finished sixth in the Premier League.

Winning the Coca-Cola Cup, selling [[Steve McAnespie]] and playing in the UEFA Cup generated the money needed to redevelop Stark's Park as an all-seater ground with North and South Stands. It was completed in time for the 1995–96 season, and Bayern Munich were invited to play a friendly in the first match in the redeveloped ground, with Raith securing a narrow 1–0 win.

===End of the fairytale===
After the club were relegated from the Premier Division, they also struggled to succeed in the First Division. For the 2001–02 season they were relegated to the Second Division for the first time since 1987. The club returned to the First Division (with the lowest winning total, to date, for champions of 59 points), under the leadership of [[Antonio Calderón]] in 2002–03 season.

At the start of the 2004–05 season, [[Claude Anelka]] (brother of French striker [[Nicolas Anelka|Nicolas]]) offered £300,000 to any team who would offer him a manager's job and was subsequently appointed the manager of Raith Rovers, with Antonio Calderón refusing the offer of a coaching role and leaving the club. Anelka signed a team of (mostly) continental players from the lower leagues in France. A disastrous season followed, despite Anelka resigning halfway through the season (replaced by [[Gordon Dalziel]]) and his signings either leaving, or having their contracts terminated, and Raith were relegated to the Second Division, after finishing bottom of the First Division with just 16 points in the season.

===Local takeover===
During 2005–06, the future of the club looked doubtful after the club, and its traditional home of [[Stark's Park]], were both placed under threat by previous owners Colin McGowan and Alex Short. The [[Glasgow]] based [[property developer]]s had repeatedly threatened to sell Stark's Park for housing in a bid to find a buyer for their 50% stake in the club and after months of legal and financial wrangling a deal was struck with their company, West City Development.

Former chairman Turnbull Hutton and director Mario Caira, who were part of West City retained their investment and were joined by major investor John Sim, a [[Thailand]]-based senior financial figure with [[liquidator (law)|liquidator]] [[KPMG]].

The ''Reclaim the Rovers'' fans' campaign, which was launched in a bid to secure a local future for the club, also secured a place for a Supporters' Representative on the new-look board after raising £100,000 towards the final figure.

On 30 December 2005, Raith Rovers' future was secured after a £1.2 million community buy-out (The New Raith Rovers Limited consortium) (assisted by the then [[Chancellor of the Exchequer]] [[Gordon Brown]] who later became [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom|Prime Minister]], a fan and shareholder<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/7939377.stm|title=Ministers reveal their interests|work=[[BBC News]]|date=12 March 2009|access-date=12 March 2009}}</ref> of the club). Previous chairman [[David Sinton]] also completed work on the takeover.

On 2 May 2009, Raith secured the [[2008–09 Scottish Second Division|Second Division title]] with a 1–0 win at the home of Scottish football, Hampden Park, with a travelling support of over 1500. They lifted the trophy in front of almost 5000 the following week following a 0–0 draw with Arbroath.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_div_1/8038849.stm|title=Raith Rovers 0–0 Arbroath
|date=9 May 2009|work=BBC Sport|access-date=26 May 2009}}</ref>

On 6 April 2014, Raith won the [[2014 Scottish Challenge Cup final]] 1–0 against [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] after extra time.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/latest/raith-rovers-1-0-rangers-aet-glory-for-raith-1-3367123|title=Glory for Raith |date=6 April 2014|work=Scotsman|access-date=8 April 2014}}</ref>

In early 2022 the club signed [[David Goodwillie]]. Days later, after an outcry regarding the rape ruling against him, chairman John Sim announced Goodwillie will not play for Raith Rovers and the club would review his contract. Raith's women's teams had moved to sever ties with the club.<ref>{{cite news |title=David Goodwillie: Raith Rovers says rapist will not play for them |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-60244442 |access-date=3 February 2022 |work=BBC News}}</ref> Goodwillie was released from his contract in September, no details being given by the club.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/david-goodwillie-released-by-raith-rovers-as-club-issue-statement-eight-months-on-from-controversial-signing-3862742|title=David Goodwillie released by Raith Rovers as club issue statement eight months on from controversial signing|date=30 September 2022|website=Scotsman.com}}</ref>

==Colours and badge==
Raith's kit consists of dark blue tops with light blue detailing, with white shorts and dark blue socks.<ref name="raithrovers.net">{{cite web|url=http://www.raithrovers.net/30351/strip-launch.htm|title=2017/18 Strips Launched - Raith Rovers FC|website=Raithrovers.net|access-date=14 August 2017|archive-date=15 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815062358/http://www.raithrovers.net/30351/strip-launch.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Raith's current badge has been used since 1998,<ref name = "HFK">{{cite web|title=Raith Rovers|url=https://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Scottish_Football_League/Raith_Rovers/Raith_Rovers.htm|publisher=Historical Football Kits|first=Dave|last=Moor|access-date=9 October 2011}}</ref> replacing the previous lion and shield motif used in different colour combinations (including being framed in a shield shape from 1995 to 1998) since 1985.<ref name="HFK"/>

==Fife rivalries==
{{Main|Fife derby}}
There are three other [[Scottish Professional Football League|SPFL]] clubs in Fife: [[East Fife F.C.|East Fife]] (based in [[Methil]]) around 8 miles to the east, with [[Kelty Hearts F.C.|Kelty Hearts]] and [[Dunfermline Athletic F.C.|Dunfermline Athletic]] 13 and 14 miles respectively to the west. Raith's traditional derby is with East Fife though the biggest rivalry is against Dunfermline, with an encounter at [[East End Park]] in April 2011 attracting a crowd of over 11,000. [[Cowdenbeath F.C.|Cowdenbeath]] dropped from the SPFL into the [[Lowland Football League|Lowland League]] in 2022 but historically were another regular derby rival in various divisions.

===Literature===
The team is often mentioned in Ian Rankin's [[Inspector Rebus]] novels, Rankin stating that Rebus is a supporter.<ref>{{Cite news  | last = Donaldson  | first = Mark  | title = Ian Rankin : Stretching the Imagination  | newspaper = The Active Nation Scottish Cup Semi-final Official Programme – Raith Rovers v Dundee United  | location = Glasgow  | pages = 34–5  | publisher = The Scottish Football Association  | date = 11 April 2010  | quote = Having gone to university in Edinburgh I didn't want Rebus to get in to that Hearts or Hibs thing that you tend to get involved in when in pubs in the capital. He's not from Edinburgh, he's from Fife, so I thought he may as well support a team that I know.}}</ref> In [[Giles Foden]]'s novel ''[[The Last King of Scotland]]'' the protagonist, Nicholas Garrigan, is a Raith Rovers fan.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dKZX7n0HRd0C&q=raith|title=The Last King of Scotland|first=Giles|last=Foden|date=4 September 2008|publisher=Faber & Faber|isbn=9780571246175|via=Google Books}}</ref>

===Music===
The Raith Rovers anthem is "Geordie Munro", with its prominent mention of Kirkcaldy.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fifetoday.co.uk/news/oh-no-no-no-a-new-geordie-munro-1-1658647|title=Oh no, no, no... a new Geordie Munro!|website=Fifetoday.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.raithrovers.net/3292/the-new-geordie-munro.htm|title=The New Geordie Munro | Raith Rovers FC|website=Raithrovers.net}}</ref>

=== Fan friendships and contacts ===
Supporter contact is maintained with fans of the German football club [[FC Ingolstadt 04]], from the twin city of [[Ingolstadt]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=achtzig20 |date=2016-01-23 |title=Schanzer zu Besuch bei den Raith Rovers in Kirkcaldy |url=https://www.fcingolstadt.de/schanzer-zu-besuch-bei-den-raith-rovers-in-kirkcaldy/ |access-date=2024-08-12 |website=FC Ingolstadt 04 |language=de-DE}}</ref>

==Managerial history==
Managers of the club have included:
* 1945–1961: [[Bert Herdman]] – Oversaw some of the club's most successful seasons and a sustained period in the top flight.
* 1964–1967, 1971–1974: [[George Farm]] – In a career of distinction in both playing and managing, Farm included a promotion success with Raith among the numerous achievements he enjoyed throughout his career.
* 1986–1990: [[Frank Connor]] – Took the club from depths of the Second Division to a solid First Division spot.
* 1990–1996: [[Jimmy Nicholl]] – Manager (and player until 1994) who won two First Division titles, the historic League Cup victory and oversaw Rovers' only foray into European competition.

Raith Rovers have appointed 34 permanent managers since [[World War II]]:<ref>{{cite web|title=Raith Rovers – Managers|url=https://www.soccerbase.com/teams/team.sd?team_id=2102&teamTabs=managers|website=Soccerbase|access-date=21 November 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Raith Rovers Managerial Timeline|url=https://www.fitbastats.com/raithrovers/manager_timeline.php|website=Fitba Stats|access-date=22 October 2024}}</ref>

==Notable former players==
===The League Cup winning team===
Players from the team that lifted the [[1994–95 Scottish League Cup]] include:
* [[Shaun Dennis]] – Over 400 appearances in three different spells between 1988 and 2004 before taking on a coaching role for a short period. Also played for [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]] and [[Brechin City F.C.|Brechin City]].
* [[Colin Cameron (footballer)|Colin Cameron]] – 'Mickey', a former Scottish internationalist who started his career with Raith Rovers. He was signed by [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Hearts]] where he won the Scottish Cup in 1998 before moving onto [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolves]], [[Coventry City F.C.|Coventry City]] and [[Milton Keynes Dons F.C.|Milton Keynes Dons]].
* [[Jason Dair]] – Experienced midfielder Dair, who can also play in defence, has also played for [[Millwall F.C.|Millwall]] and [[Dunfermline Athletic F.C.|Dunfermline]], among many other teams. Like his one-time teammate, Shaun Dennis, Jason had three different spells at Raith.
* [[Stevie Crawford]] – A former Scottish international who started his career with Raith Rovers. He played for [[Cowdenbeath FC|Cowdenbeath]] after being released from his second spell with [[Dunfermline Athletic F.C.|Dunfermline]]. Crawford has also played for [[Millwall F.C.|Millwall]], [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]], [[Plymouth Argyle F.C.|Plymouth Argyle]], [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]], [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]] and [[East Fife F.C.|East Fife]] (Was also manager of the latter club).
* [[Gordon Dalziel]] – Record league goalscorer for Raith Rovers with 154 goals in the 1980s and 1990s, who returned as a manager in 2004. Scored the equalising goal in the Cup Final.
* [[David Narey|David Narey MBE]] – veteran player, formerly of [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]] (1973–1994), who scored a goal against [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]] in the [[1982 FIFA World Cup|1982 World Cup]]. David retired after the Coca-Cola Cup win, in which he was named Man of the Match.
* [[Steve McAnespie]] – Sold to [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]] for Raith's record transfer fee of £900,000 at the end of the 1994–95 season. Now coaching in the US. The money from his transfer helped redevelop [[Stark's Park]].

Also involved in the squad were [[Scott Y. Thomson|Scott Thomson]], [[Julian Broddle]], [[David Sinclair (footballer, born 1969)|David Sinclair]], [[Ally Graham]], [[Brian Potter (footballer)|Brian Potter]], [[Jason Rowbotham]] and [[Ian Redford (footballer)|Ian Redford]].

* Record defeat: 2–11 vs [[Greenock Morton F.C.|Morton]], Division 2, 1936
* League goalscoring record: Norrie Heywood, 1937–38, 42 goals
* Most league goals (individual): [[Gordon Dalziel]], 154 (1987–1994)
* Most goals in a league season (team): 142, 1937–38 (British Record)
* Most capped player: David Morris, 6 caps for [[Scotland national football team|Scotland]]
* Highest transfer fee paid: £225,000 for Paul Harvey (from [[Airdrie United F.C.|Airdrie]], July 1996)
* Highest transfer fee received: £900,000 for [[Steve McAnespie]] (to [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]], September 1995)
